title: Serving the nagar kirtan
hook: families serve food and water along the procession route
tomorrow: it's June, it's hot, and a stranger hands you a free drink. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, prabhat pheri: hymns carried door to door before sunrise. Singing at dawn. By midday the full procession is moving, and the sidewalks have changed.

On a nagar kirtan route, it starts with folding tables. Families set them up along the sidewalk: steel pots, coolers, paper plates, a banner with the family's name. By noon, someone walking the route can be handed pakoras, fruit, juice, chai, ice cream, a full plate of rice and dal. Free, to anyone. And every year, somewhere in the sangat, someone asks out loud: is this getting out of hand?
screen: `FOLDING TABLES ALONG THE ROUTE.` → `FREE, TO ANYONE.` → `IS THIS GETTING OUT OF HAND?`

segments.voice: That question is a real conversation among Sikhs, and both sides have a strong case. The case for plenty first. Langar has a generous history. In the Ramkali ki Var, the bards Satta and Balvand praise Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife, whose langar served rich kheer made with ghee. Serving the road with plenty says: in the Guru's house nobody leaves hungry, and nobody is too poor for the good food. Families who have served the same corner for years feel it as their seva, and their joy. Now the case for simple. Some sangats and Sikh writers ask for fewer stalls and simpler food: less plastic, less waste, less of a food fair. Their point is the center. A nagar kirtan is kirtan: the Guru Granth Sahib carried through town with the sangat singing behind. If the crowd follows the dessert tables, the Guru passes by unnoticed. And one thing both sides already share is the road itself. Volunteers walk ahead of the palki, sweeping and washing the street, so the Guru travels a clean path. Whatever ends up on the tables, the serving starts with a broom.
screen: `THE CASE FOR PLENTY: MATA KHIVI'S KHEER.` · `THE CASE FOR SIMPLE: KEEP THE CENTER.` · `BOTH SWEEP AHEAD OF THE PALKI.` · then, large: `SERVE THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Sit up and hold both hands out in front of you, palms up, as if offering a cup to someone walking past. Stay in that posture for the sit, breathing slowly. Notice what it's like to keep your hands open with no idea who the next person will be.
Serving the nagar kirtan. Setting up along the procession route to feed, water and clean up after it: seva done on the street, for anyone.
Something to keep: serve the road, the people on it and the street beneath them. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: our stall is done but the route is covered in cups and plates. dad says we're finished. are we?
options: Not yet. The road is part of the seva; sweep up behind the Guru like they swept ahead.
Yes. The city crews clean up; your seva was the food, and that part is done.
Only if the gurdwara asks. Cleanup belongs to the sevadars in charge of it.
chat.meaning: Serving the nagar kirtan starts with sweeping the road ahead of the palki. The street is part of the seva, after the food too.

nagar kirtan.meaning: a procession singing the Guru's hymns through a town

Ramkali ki Var.meaning: a ballad in Raag Ramkali by the bards Satta and Balvand

Mata Khivi.meaning: Guru Angad's wife, remembered for running the langar

langar.meaning: the Guru's free kitchen, open to everyone

palki.meaning: the canopied seat that carries the Guru Granth Sahib
